opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the key insight is that it reframes what problem we actually need to solve. If you think about aligning superintelligence directly, that's this enormously daunting task. You're trying to figure out how to supervise systems that might be vastly smarter than you, that might be thinking about things you can't even conceptualize. And it's really hard to make concrete progress on that today, because we don't have those systems, and we don't really know what they'll look like.

But if you scope it down and say, "Okay, what we actually need to do is align a system that's roughly as capable as us at doing alignment research," that's a much more tractable problem. It's a system that's not that different from the systems we have today, or the ones we'll have in a few years. We can study it empirically. We can iterate on it. And crucially, we can still evaluate a lot of what it's doing, because it's roughly at our level.

And then the idea is that once you have that system, it can help you with the next step. You can have many copies of it working in parallel, working really fast, and they can do the alignment research needed for the next generation of systems, which are a bit more capable, and so on. So you don't have to solve the whole problem yourself up front. You kind of hand off more and more of the work, in a careful way.

The other reason I find it encouraging is that evaluation is generally easier than generation. Even if we can't come up with the solution ourselves, it's often much easier for us to look at a proposed solution and check whether it makes sense, especially with AI assistance in doing that checking. So that asymmetry works in our favor.

Now, I don't want to oversell it. There are a lot of ways this could go wrong. You have to actually make sure the system is aligned and not just appearing aligned, and you have to be careful that you're not bootstrapping your way into something you no longer understand. But compared to trying to solve the whole thing in one shot, it feels like a problem where we can actually make progress, and that's a big reason why I'm more optimistic than I would otherwise be.

r001.rationale: It says the goal is to align a system roughly as capable as people doing alignment research, and describes it as being roughly at our level.

r002.rationale: It says an aligned system could help with the next step by doing alignment research for more capable systems.

r003.rationale: It contrasts this tractable target with aligning superintelligence directly, which it describes as vastly smarter and much harder to supervise.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the way I think about it is that we don't actually have to solve the whole problem ourselves. The core realisation is that the hardest version of alignment — aligning a system that is vastly superhuman, where we can't check its work or even really understand what it's doing — that's not the first problem we face. The first problem we face is a much easier one, which is: can we align a system that is roughly at the level of a good alignment researcher?

And that's a system that is much more within reach for us to study, to evaluate, and to supervise, because it's doing things that we as humans can still follow. If it writes a paper or proposes an experiment or writes some interpretability code, we can read it, we can critique it, we can run it and see if it works. We're not completely out of our depth yet. So all the techniques we have today — reinforcement learning from human feedback, scalable oversight, red teaming, interpretability — are much more applicable to that regime than to a wildly superhuman one.

And if we can get that system to a point where we really trust it to do alignment research honestly and well, then the game changes, because now we're not limited by the number of humans who happen to work on this. You can run thousands of copies of it, they can work around the clock, and you can basically turn compute into alignment progress. So the problem goes from "a few hundred researchers have to figure out everything before timelines run out" to "we have to get one roughly human-level system right, and then it helps us with the next step."

Now, I want to be careful here. It's not a free lunch. You have to actually succeed at aligning that first system, and you need to be able to tell whether it's really aligned versus just telling you what you want to hear. That's the crux, and that's where a lot of our effort goes. But I think it's a much more tractable problem than the one people usually picture when they imagine aligning superintelligence from scratch. It's a bootstrapping story, and each step along the way you have a system that's only a bit more capable than what you can already evaluate. That's what makes me optimistic — not that the whole thing is easy, but that the first step is one we might actually be able to take.

r001.rationale: It identifies the first alignment goal as a system roughly at the level of a good alignment researcher, rather than a vastly superhuman system.

r002.rationale: It says that once such a system is trusted to do alignment research, many copies could work on it and turn compute into alignment progress.

r003.rationale: It explains that researcher-level systems remain possible for humans to study, evaluate, and supervise, making this a more tractable problem than aligning superintelligence from scratch.

astra-6.text:
Well, if we can align a system that’s roughly as smart as the best alignment researchers, then we can use it to help us solve the next stage of alignment. We don’t necessarily have to solve the whole problem of aligning arbitrarily capable systems in one go.

Imagine having many copies of a really good alignment researcher working together. They could help us come up with better techniques, find flaws in our approaches, and run experiments. And because they’re working at a level we can still understand, we have a better chance of evaluating whether they’re making real progress.

Then we could use that work to align a somewhat more capable system, and use that system to help with the next step. That’s the bootstrapping picture that makes me optimistic: the tools available to us for solving alignment can get better as AI gets better.

Of course, that isn’t a guarantee. We still have to align that first system, and we need to be able to trust and evaluate the research it produces. But it means humans might not have to figure out the entire solution unaided.

r001.rationale: It identifies the first system to align as roughly as smart as the best alignment researchers.

r002.rationale: It says the aligned system could help develop techniques, find flaws, and run experiments for alignment research.

r003.rationale: It contrasts aligning a researcher-level system with solving alignment for arbitrarily capable systems all at once, and says the researcher-level system would be easier to understand and evaluate.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, because at that point you can get the system to help you with alignment research. Right now, the number of people working on this problem is pretty small. If you had an AI that was as good at alignment research as the best humans, you could potentially run lots of copies of it and make much faster progress.

So you don’t necessarily have to solve the whole problem of aligning arbitrarily superhuman systems ourselves. You need to figure out how to align a system that’s capable enough to help you solve the next stage of the problem. Then you can use that help to work out how to align more capable systems.

Of course, there’s a big catch: you need to be able to trust the research it’s doing. If it gives you a proposed solution, how do you tell whether that solution actually works, or whether it’s hiding something you wouldn’t notice? So this doesn’t make the problem go away. But it gives us a route where increasingly capable AI is also increasingly useful for solving alignment, rather than just making the problem harder.

r001.rationale: The response describes an AI as good at alignment research as the best humans and says the goal is to align a system capable enough to help with the next stage.

r002.rationale: It says an AI matching the best humans at alignment research could be copied to make faster progress on alignment.

r003.rationale: It contrasts aligning a system that can help with the next stage against having to solve alignment for arbitrarily superhuman systems, presenting the staged approach as a route forward.
